name: sand3d
description: 3D modeling in Python, built for LLMs.
readmeExcerpt:
sand3d

**3D modeling in Python, built for LLMs.** sand3d is a Python library for writing 3D objects as short programs: profiles, solids, edits, frames, joints and assemblies, and the forms of nature (grass, moss, trees, water, rock), over Blender's `bpy`. A program says *how* a shape is made, part by part and in its own words, so a model writes it in a few hundred tokens and a person can read it.

 Website ·  Docs ·  Datasets ·  Explorer

## Why sand3d


How it is measured, part by part

- **Short.** A part takes 2 to 6× fewer tokens than the same part in Blender Python, CadQuery or FeatureScript ([details](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/tokens.html)). - **One file to prompt.** Every signature, one line each, in [the API](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/api.html); a short guide per technique (water, trees, terrain…) is read only when a task needs it. - **Named, not computed.** Parts, edges and faces are reached by name, never by hand-computed coordinates. - **Deterministic.** The same program builds the same mesh, bit for bit, in the same environment. ## A whole object, part by part

A front-loading washing machine in 38 lines of code ([play it and read it](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/gallery.html)): the cabinet, the drum, the door with its glass and handle, the detergent drawer and the dial, each a named part, and four joints that say how they move. ```python door = s3d.group("door", ring, glass, handle) # the handle and the glass move with it s3d.joint("door_hinge", door, hinge, axis="-Z", range=(0, 143)) s3d.joint("drum_spin", drum, front.move(0, 400), kind="continuous") s3d.joint("drawer_slide", drawer, top_band.move(150), kind="prismatic", axis="+X", range=(0, 200)) s3d.joint("dial_turn", dial, top_band.move(-150), kind="continuous") return s3d.assembly("washing_machine", cab, drum, door, drawer, dial, front=front) ``` ## Export: GLB, URDF, USD, IFC, OBJ, STL One call; the file's extension names the format; lengths in metres. ```python s3d.export(machine, "washer.glb") # or .urdf, .usda, .ifc, .obj, .stl ``` | format | what it carries | for | |---|---|---| | **GLB** | meshes, materials, the joints in each node's extras, at the current pose; points, spots and suns, their size in extras | the web, viewers, game engines | | **URDF** | a link per moving part, its joints and their limits, at rest; OBJ meshes beside it | ROS, PyBullet, MuJoCo, Isaac | | **USDA** | the same tree in OpenUSD (UsdGeom, UsdPhysics), with the materials and every light (UsdLux) | Omniverse, Isaac Sim, USD pipelines | | **IFC** | the part tree as an IFC4 project — assemblies, a proxy per part, triangulated face sets, the materials, a light fixture per point or spot | Revit, ArchiCAD, Tekla, BIM | | **OBJ** | meshes in the root's tree at the current pose, Y up, with a mean colour per part for callable colours | any 3D tool | | **STL** | meshes in the root's tree at the current pose, binary, Z up | any 3D tool, slicers | `.usd`, `.usdc` and `.usdz` come from the `.usda` through USD's own tools (`usdcat`, `usdzip`). Revit's own `.rvt` is written by Revit alone — no library writes one — so `export` names `.ifc` for it, the open standard (ISO 16739) Revit opens and links. `export` writes meshes and sand3d lights where the format supports them. Curves, text objects and anything else added with raw `bpy` are left out. Convert them to meshes first, or use Blender's own exporters. GLB, URDF and USDA also follow joints to parts outside the root's tree. IFC, OBJ and STL follow Blender parenting only. IFC exports the current pose, without joints. Its `GlobalId` values depend on geometry and placement: editing or moving a part can change its ID, and identical parts in separate models can share one. Do not use them to track parts across exports. ## Install Python 3.13 (recommended) or 3.11. Blender comes with it, as the `bpy` module: 5.2 LTS on Python 3.13, 4.5 LTS on Python 3.11; CI runs bpy 5.2. NumPy ships with the `bpy` dependency; no other dependency is needed. ```bash pip install sand3d # or, in a uv project: uv add sand3d ``` `bpy` has no wheel for Python 3.12, nor for Intel Macs from 5.2 on: there, use Python 3.11. ## A first program ```python import sand3d as s3d def bracket(w=80, d=40, t=6, hole_d=6.6, pitch=50): plate = s3d.extrude("plate", s3d.rect(w, d, r=4), t) s3d.hole(plate, hole_d, on=s3d.grid(2, 1, pitch, 0)) s3d.fillet(plate, 1, edges="top") return plate s3d.export(bracket(), "bracket.glb") ``` Millimetres by default. Every verb with code that runs and its render: [the quickstart](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/quickstart.html); objects to play joint by joint: [the gallery](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/gallery.html); every signature: [the API](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/api.html). The programs themselves: [docs/examples/](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/tree/main/docs/examples/) and [programs/](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/tree/main/programs/). ## Give it to your LLM Put [docs/api.md](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/blob/main/docs/api.md) in the system prompt: the rules of the vocabulary, every signature, and worked examples; [llms.txt](https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d/blob/main/llms.txt) points a model at it, and at the task guides it reads on demand. For objects of several parts, [the guidelines](https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/guidelines.html) give the eight rules of an assembly program: the plan first, then the details, then the parts. ## What is in it Everything on one flat `s3d.` surface: | family | verbs | |---|---| | profiles | `rect` `circle` `slot` `polygon` `poly` `arc` `spline` `superellipse` `text` `offset` `stroke` … (16) | | solids and paths | `extrude` `revolve` `sweep` `loft` `wire` `helix` `box` `cylinder` `tube` `sphere` `torus` `dome` `hull` `field` `fill` `waves` … (19) | | edits | `cut` `join` `intersect` `split` `hole` `pocket` `fillet` `chamfer` `shell` `dent` `bend` `twist` `taper` `displace` `smooth` `blend` … (21) | | frames and placement | `Frame` `face` `edge` `bbox` `local` `at` `transform` `grid` `ring` `along` `snap` `lay` | | distributions | `Frames` `scatter` `tufts` `branches` `phyllotaxis` `spiral` `vary` `noise` (8) | | articulation | `joint` `pose` `seat` | | assembly | `group` `assembly` `attach` `export` `units` `fingerprint` … (8) | | parts, materials and lights | `gear` `knurl` `thread` `material` `light` | No category verbs (`chair()`, `table()`): a category is a program written *in* sand3d. ## Datasets sand3d programs for six sources of 3D objects, on Hugging Face under CC BY 4.0.

sand3d

3D modeling in Python, built for LLMs.

sand3d is a Python library for writing 3D objects as short programs: profiles, solids, edits, frames, joints and assemblies, and the forms of nature (grass, moss, trees, water, rock), over Blender's bpy. A program says how a shape is made, part by part and in its own words, so a model writes it in a few hundred tokens and a person can read it.

 Website ·  Docs ·  Datasets ·  Explorer

Why sand3d


How it is measured, part by part

  • Short. A part takes 2 to 6× fewer tokens than the same part in Blender Python, CadQuery or FeatureScript (details).
  • One file to prompt. Every signature, one line each, in the API; a short guide per technique (water, trees, terrain…) is read only when a task needs it.
  • Named, not computed. Parts, edges and faces are reached by name, never by hand-computed coordinates.
  • Deterministic. The same program builds the same mesh, bit for bit, in the same environment.

A whole object, part by part

A front-loading washing machine in 38 lines of code (play it and read it): the cabinet, the drum, the door with its glass and handle, the detergent drawer and the dial, each a named part, and four joints that say how they move.

door = s3d.group("door", ring, glass, handle)                      # the handle and the glass move with it
s3d.joint("door_hinge", door, hinge, axis="-Z", range=(0, 143))
s3d.joint("drum_spin", drum, front.move(0, 400), kind="continuous")
s3d.joint("drawer_slide", drawer, top_band.move(150), kind="prismatic", axis="+X", range=(0, 200))
s3d.joint("dial_turn", dial, top_band.move(-150), kind="continuous")
return s3d.assembly("washing_machine", cab, drum, door, drawer, dial, front=front)

Export: GLB, URDF, USD, IFC, OBJ, STL

One call; the file's extension names the format; lengths in metres.

s3d.export(machine, "washer.glb")    # or .urdf, .usda, .ifc, .obj, .stl
format what it carries for
GLB meshes, materials, the joints in each node's extras, at the current pose; points, spots and suns, their size in extras the web, viewers, game engines
URDF a link per moving part, its joints and their limits, at rest; OBJ meshes beside it ROS, PyBullet, MuJoCo, Isaac
USDA the same tree in OpenUSD (UsdGeom, UsdPhysics), with the materials and every light (UsdLux) Omniverse, Isaac Sim, USD pipelines
IFC the part tree as an IFC4 project — assemblies, a proxy per part, triangulated face sets, the materials, a light fixture per point or spot Revit, ArchiCAD, Tekla, BIM
OBJ meshes in the root's tree at the current pose, Y up, with a mean colour per part for callable colours any 3D tool
STL meshes in the root's tree at the current pose, binary, Z up any 3D tool, slicers

.usd, .usdc and .usdz come from the .usda through USD's own tools (usdcat, usdzip). Revit's own .rvt is written by Revit alone — no library writes one — so export names .ifc for it, the open standard (ISO 16739) Revit opens and links.

export writes meshes and sand3d lights where the format supports them. Curves, text objects and anything else added with raw bpy are left out. Convert them to meshes first, or use Blender's own exporters.

GLB, URDF and USDA also follow joints to parts outside the root's tree. IFC, OBJ and STL follow Blender parenting only.

IFC exports the current pose, without joints. Its GlobalId values depend on geometry and placement: editing or moving a part can change its ID, and identical parts in separate models can share one. Do not use them to track parts across exports.

Install

Python 3.13 (recommended) or 3.11. Blender comes with it, as the bpy module: 5.2 LTS on Python 3.13, 4.5 LTS on Python 3.11; CI runs bpy 5.2. NumPy ships with the bpy dependency; no other dependency is needed.

pip install sand3d        # or, in a uv project: uv add sand3d

bpy has no wheel for Python 3.12, nor for Intel Macs from 5.2 on: there, use Python 3.11.

A first program

import sand3d as s3d

def bracket(w=80, d=40, t=6, hole_d=6.6, pitch=50):
    plate = s3d.extrude("plate", s3d.rect(w, d, r=4), t)
    s3d.hole(plate, hole_d, on=s3d.grid(2, 1, pitch, 0))
    s3d.fillet(plate, 1, edges="top")
    return plate

s3d.export(bracket(), "bracket.glb")

Millimetres by default. Every verb with code that runs and its render: the quickstart; objects to play joint by joint: the gallery; every signature: the API. The programs themselves: docs/examples/ and programs/.

Give it to your LLM

Put docs/api.md in the system prompt: the rules of the vocabulary, every signature, and worked examples; llms.txt points a model at it, and at the task guides it reads on demand. For objects of several parts, the guidelines give the eight rules of an assembly program: the plan first, then the details, then the parts.

What is in it

Everything on one flat s3d.<verb> surface:

family verbs
profiles rect circle slot polygon poly arc spline superellipse text offset stroke … (16)
solids and paths extrude revolve sweep loft wire helix box cylinder tube sphere torus dome hull field fill waves … (19)
edits cut join intersect split hole pocket fillet chamfer shell dent bend twist taper displace smooth blend … (21)
frames and placement Frame face edge bbox local at transform grid ring along snap lay
distributions Frames scatter tufts branches phyllotaxis spiral vary noise (8)
articulation joint pose seat
assembly group assembly attach export units fingerprint … (8)
parts, materials and lights gear knurl thread material light

No category verbs (chair(), table()): a category is a program written in sand3d.

Datasets

sand3d programs for six sources of 3D objects, on Hugging Face under CC BY 4.0.


sand3d-objaverse · Objaverse
Everyday objects from Objaverse, each rebuilt as a program.
sand3d-cad · CAD
Mechanical parts from public CAD models.
sand3d-articraft · Articraft
Articulated objects from Articraft, their joints declared.

sand3d-simready · SimReady
Simulation-ready assets from NVIDIA SimReady.
sand3d-automate · AutoMate
Mechanical assemblies from AutoMate, each part a function of its program.
sand3d-nature · Nature
Plants, trees, rocks, corals and fungi, built with the organic verbs.

Browse them in the explorer, or all six in the collection.

Citation

If you use sand3d in your work, please cite it. CITATION.cff holds the same, and GitHub shows it as "Cite this repository".

@misc{sand3d2026,
  author = {Neveu, Thibault and Loy, Andr{\'e}a},
  title  = {sand3d},
  year   = {2026},
  note   = {Version 1.7.0},
  url    = {https://github.com/Sandflow-ai/sand3d}
}

Contributing and license

How the library is built, tested and versioned: CONTRIBUTING.md. Apache License 2.0: see LICENSE.

releases.name: sand3d 1.7.0
releases.body:
### Features

* Organic modelling: implicit fields, deformers (`displace`, `bend`, `twist`, `taper`,
  `dent`, `blend`), seeded scatter, branching and phyllotaxis, `snap` and `lay` onto another
  surface, rooted blades and fur with `tufts`, colour functions, optical media, and task
  guides for nature (#44)
* Lights in lumens and lux, written by every export that can carry them (#43, fixes #38)
* A corner radius too large for its side is clamped with a warning, and a loft section that
  crosses itself says where (#42, fixes #41)
* `export` writes a trace of what was built beside the file (#31)
* A cut, hole or pocket that misses warns by default; strict mode raises (#36)
* `copy(ob, name=…)` names a copy, and the parts and joints it holds (#30)
* `facets` sets the segments of a full circle (#19)
* `export` writes `.ifc`, and names it for Revit's `.rvt` (#12)

### Fixes

* `export` says which meshes it writes (#47)
* Binary STL headers no longer start with `solid` (#45)
* Text files are read and written as UTF-8 (#34)
* An empty intersection warns (#18, fixes #14)
* A solid with a long name builds, and keeps its face and edge names (#20, fixes #13)

### Behaviour changes

* `facets

releases.name: sand3d 1.6.3
releases.body:
### Fixes

* A GLB holds only the root's tree, in metres: the rest of the scene no longer comes
  along, and a placed or mirrored root keeps its offset and its mirror (#11, fixes #10)

Thanks to @alaabenfatma for the report and the fix.

Install: `pip install sand3d` · Website: https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/

releases.name: sand3d 1.6.1
releases.body:
First public release of sand3d: profiles, solids, edits, frames, joints and an
assembly layer over Blender's `bpy`, with export to GLB, URDF, USD (`.usda`,
UsdPhysics), OBJ and STL. `pip install sand3d` brings the `bpy` its Python takes:
bpy 4.5 on Python 3.11, bpy 5.2 on Python 3.13. The API is described in
[docs/api.md](docs/api.md).

Install: `pip install sand3d` · Website: https://sand3d.sandflow.ai/

aiSummary.oneLiner: Toolkit for generating and manipulating 3D models using AI.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: Sand3d provides tools and pipelines for integrating generative AI models with 3D workflows. It facilitates the conversion of text prompts or 2D images into textured 3D assets. The project handles mesh generation, UV mapping, and texture synthesis. It aims to accelerate asset creation for game development and virtual reality. The toolkit can be integrated into existing DCC applications like Blender.
keyFeatures: Text-to-3D generation: creates initial 3D meshes from descriptive text prompts.
Image-to-3D conversion: extrudes and textures models based on reference 2D images.
Automatic UV unwrapping: generates optimized UV layouts for AI-generated textures.
Format export: supports exporting assets to standard formats like GLTF and OBJ.
Pipeline integration: provides APIs for embedding generation capabilities into other tools.

useCases.description: Rapidly prototype 3D props and environments for game development.

useCases.description: Generate optimized assets for immersive VR experiences.
